It’s known mostly for its leafy streets and posh homes, sitting close to Highgate and not far from Parliament Hill, where you get cracking views of the city.

name: National Covid Memorial Wall
summary:
The National Covid Memorial Wall in London is a public memorial painted by volunteers to commemorate victims of the COVID-19 pandemic in the United Kingdom. Started in March 2021 and stretching more than one-third of a mile (540 metres) along the South Bank of the River Thames, opposite the Palace of Westminster, the memorial consists of over 250,000 red hearts, one for each person in the United Kingdom who died with COVID-19 on their death certificate.
In June 2025, The National Covid Memorial Wall became a registered charity with the Charity Commission for England and Wales.
script: The National Covid Memorial Wall is right along the South Bank, just opposite the Houses of Parliament—a spot where you can’t miss it if you’re walking by the Thames. It’s covered in over 250,000 red hearts, each one painted by volunteers to remember someone who sadly passed away during the pandemic.

name: Odeon Luxe West End
summary:
The Odeon Luxe West End is a two-screen cinema on the south side of Leicester Square, London. It has historically been used for smaller film premieres and hosting the annual BFI London Film Festival. The site is on an adjacent side of the square to the much larger flagship Odeon Luxe Leicester Square.
Odeon Cinemas sold the building to three Irish investors in 2006, who continued to lease it. In 2012, it was bought by the Radisson Edwardian hotel group. It closed as a cinema on 1 January 2015. After extensive asbestos removal, the entire site was demolished the same year.
It reopened in September 2021 as an Odeon Luxe cinema, following a £300 million redevelopment of the site that also includes a luxury hotel. It is London's second Dolby Cinema.
script: The Odeon Luxe West End is a swanky two-screen cinema right on the south side of Leicester Square, just a stone’s throw from the bigger Odeon Luxe Leicester Square. It’s known for smaller premieres and hosting parts of the London Film Festival, but what most folks don’t realise is that the whole place was completely knocked down in 2015 because of asbestos, then rebuilt from scratch as part of a posh £300 million makeover.

name: Unit London
summary: Unit is a contemporary art gallery based at 3 Hanover Square in Mayfair, London, with a secondary location, The Stables, in Covent Garden. It was founded by two young artists, Joe Kennedy and Jonny Burt, in 2013.
script: The Unit London gallery is a contemporary art spot right in the heart of Mayfair, just off Hanover Square, which is pretty posh for art these days. It started out as a tiny pop-up in Chiswick back in 2013, run by two young artists who really knew how to use social media to make a name for themselves—quite clever, considering most galleries are pretty old-fashioned.

name: Kensal Town
summary: Kensal Town is a district located partly in the Royal Borough of Kensington and Chelsea, and partly in the City of Westminster. The Grand Union Canal, which passes through it, forms the boundary of the two boroughs. Kensal Town is a sub-district of Kensal Green. The area lies four miles north-west of Charing Cross and is part of the W postcode area. Kensal Town was an exclave of Chelsea from the middle ages through to 1900.
script: The Kensal Town area sits about four miles northwest of Charing Cross, straddling the border between Kensington and Chelsea and the City of Westminster, right by the Grand Union Canal. It’s got a proper old-school vibe because back in the day, it was called Chelsea-in-the-Wilderness—oak trees from there were even used to build Westminster Abbey, believe it or not.

name: Maryland
summary: Maryland is a neighbourhood in Stratford in London, United Kingdom. It is in the London Borough of Newham. The community centres around Maryland Station and borders Leytonstone to the north, Stratford New Town to the west and Forest Gate to the east, with Stratford town centre to the south-west.
script: The Maryland area is a little neighbourhood just north-east of Stratford, right in Newham, and it’s centred around Maryland Station. Now, you might think it’s named after the American state, and there’s a story about a merchant who came back from Maryland and set up shop here, but historians aren’t so sure. Some reckon the name actually comes from old English words meaning a boundary—so it’s more homegrown than colonial.

name: Queer Britain
summary: Queer Britain is a museum of British LGBTQ history and culture located in Kings Cross, London. It is the first dedicated LGBTQ museum in the UK. The museum consists of three connected galleries plus a shop and occupies the ground floor of 2 Granary Square, a building owned by the Art Fund, with office and studio space on lower ground. Admission is free.
script: The Queer Britain museum’s right in King’s Cross, just by Granary Square, and it’s the UK’s very first museum dedicated entirely to LGBTQ history and culture. Now, a lot of folks might not know this, but it actually started out without a permanent home, putting on pop-up shows around London before settling into its proper spot in 2022.

name: Gordon Museum
summary: The Gordon Museum of Pathology is a medical museum that is part of King's College London in London, England. It is one of the largest pathology museums in the world and is the largest medical museum in the United Kingdom. Its primary function is to train medical, dental, biomedical and healthcare students and professionals to diagnose diseases.
script: The Gordon Museum is a fascinating medical museum tucked inside King’s College London, near the Strand in central London. It’s actually the biggest medical museum in the UK and holds thousands of specimens that help teach doctors about diseases. What many don’t know is that some of the specimens date back over 400 years – that’s older than most of the buildings around here!

name: Three Mills
summary:
The Three Mills are former working mills and an island of the same name on the River Lea. It is one of London’s oldest surviving industrial centres. The mills lie in the London Borough of Newham, but despite lying on the Newham side of the Lea, access is principally from the western, London Borough of Tower Hamlets, side of the river.
The River Lea Tidal Mill Trust Ltd owns the House Mill and the Miller's House buildings, which are used for educational projects and as conference spaces. The Lower Lea Project is also based at Three Mills in The Miller's House.
script: The Three Mills are old tidal mills on the River Lea, just east of central London in Newham, though you actually get to them from Tower Hamlets. They’re some of the oldest surviving industrial buildings in London, dating back to medieval times when they ground flour for London’s bakers. A bit of a surprise is that one of the mills was once used to make gunpowder back in the 16th century—so not just bread and pastries!

name: Waterloo
summary: Waterloo () is a district in Central London, and part of the Waterloo and South Bank ward of the London Borough of Lambeth. It is situated 1 mile (1.6 km) east of Charing Cross. The area is part of a business improvement district which includes The Cut and the Old Vic and Young Vic theatres. It includes some sections of the London Borough of Southwark.
script: The Waterloo district is right in Central London, just about a mile east of Charing Cross, near the South Bank by the Thames. It’s best known for the big Waterloo Station and the Old Vic theatre, a proper cultural hub. But many don’t realise the area used to be marshland called Lambeth Marshe before it was drained in the 18th century—so it wasn’t always the bustling spot it is today.

name: Gants Hill
summary: Gants Hill is an area of Ilford in East London, England, within the borough of Redbridge. It is a suburb 9.5 miles (15.3 km) east northeast of Charing Cross. It lends its name to a central roundabout where five roads meet.
script: The Gants Hill roundabout is a busy spot out East, about nine miles from central London, right in Ilford. Most folks know it as just a tricky junction where five roads meet, but not many realise it’s named after the le Gant family, who were stewards to Barking Abbey way back in medieval times.

name: London Stone
summary:
London Stone is a historic landmark housed at 111 Cannon Street in the City of London. It is an irregular block of oolitic limestone measuring 53 × 43 × 30 cm (21 × 17 × 12"), the remnant of a once much larger object that had stood for many centuries on the south side of the street.
The name "London Stone" was first recorded around the year 1100. The date and original purpose of the stone are unknown, although it is possibly of Roman origin. There has been interest and speculation about it since the medieval period, but modern claims that it was formerly an object of veneration, or has some occult significance, are unsubstantiated.
script: The London Stone is a curious little landmark tucked away on Cannon Street, right in the heart of the City of London. It’s this old block of limestone that’s been there for centuries, possibly since Roman times, though nobody’s quite sure what it was originally for.

name: St Michael Cornhill War Memorial
summary: St Michael Cornhill War Memorial is a First World War memorial by the entrance to the church of St Michael Cornhill, facing Cornhill in the City of London.  The memorial became a Grade II* listed building in December 2016 ; the church itself is Grade I listed.
script: The St Michael Cornhill War Memorial stands just outside the church of the same name, right in the heart of the City of London. It’s a striking tribute to over two thousand local men who served in the First World War, with the angelic figure of Archangel Michael wielding a flaming sword at the top.

name: Kennington Cross
summary:
Kennington Cross is a locality in the London Borough of Lambeth.
It is at the junction of two major roads, Kennington Lane that links Vauxhall Cross with the Elephant and Castle and Kennington Road that runs from Waterloo to Kennington Park.
At the junction are the Durning Library (London Borough of Lambeth), St Anselm's Church (Church of England) and The ArtsLav project, a nineteenth-century underground gents Victorian Lavatory converted into a small local arts venue. 
There are two large public houses, The Dog House, and The Tommyfield.
script: The Kennington Cross is a little spot down in Lambeth where two busy roads meet—Kennington Lane and Kennington Road, just a short hop from Waterloo and the Elephant and Castle. You’ll find the Durning Library and St Anselm’s Church here, but what’s really quite quirky is the ArtsLav project: an old Victorian underground gents’ lavatory that’s been turned into an arts venue. Not many Londoners know that!

name: Queen Eleanor Memorial Cross
summary:
The Queen Eleanor Memorial Cross is a memorial to Eleanor of Castile erected in the forecourt of Charing Cross railway station, London, in 1864–1865. It is a fanciful reconstruction of the medieval Eleanor cross at Charing, one of twelve memorial crosses erected by Edward I of England in memory of his first wife. The Victorian monument was designed by Edward Middleton Barry, also the architect of the railway station, and includes multiple statues of Queen Eleanor by the sculptor Thomas Earp. It is located 200 metres (220 yd) northeast of the original site of the Charing Cross (destroyed in 1647), which is now occupied by Hubert Le Sueur's equestrian statue of Charles I, installed in 1675; both are along the Strand roadway.
Barry based the memorial on the three surviving drawings of the Charing Cross, in the Bodleian Library, the British Museum and the collection of the Royal Society of Antiquaries. However, due to the fragmentary nature of this evidence, he also drew from a wider range of sources including the other surviving Eleanor crosses and Queen Eleanor's tomb at Westminster Abbey. In this search for precedents Barry was assisted by his fellow architect Arthur Ashpitel. The coats of arms of England, León, Castile and Ponthieu appear on the monument.
script: The Queen Eleanor Memorial Cross is this beautiful Victorian monument just outside Charing Cross station, right in the heart of London near the Strand. It’s actually a bit of a clever ‘what if’—a recreation of the original medieval cross that King Edward I had built for his wife Eleanor, but that was knocked down way back in the 1600s.

name: John Donne Memorial
summary:
The John Donne Memorial is a bronze bust of John Donne by Nigel Boonham, installed in the garden to the south of St Paul's Cathedral in London, United Kingdom. Donne faces east towards his birthplace on Bread Street. Below the bust is an inscription with the text

It was commissioned by the City of London, led by Alderman Robert Hall, and marks the first public memorial to Donne.
script: The John Donne Memorial is a bronze bust tucked away in the garden just south of St Paul’s Cathedral, right in the heart of the City. What’s clever is that Donne’s bust is actually facing east, staring straight at the spot where he was born on Bread Street. Not many folks know it’s the very first public memorial to him, only put up fairly recently thanks to a City alderman’s push.

name: Edward VI
summary: The statue of Edward VI by Thomas Cartwright at St Thomas' Hospital, Lambeth, London is one of two statues of that king at the hospital. Both commemorate Edward's re-founding of the institution in 1551. The statue was designed by Nathaniel Hanwell and carved by Thomas Cartwright in 1682, during the rebuilding undertaken by Sir Robert Clayton when President of the hospital. The statue originally formed the centrepiece of a group of figures which adorned the gateway on Borough High Street. It was moved to its current location at the north entrance to the North Wing on Lambeth Palace Road in the 20th century. It was designated a Grade II* listed structure in 1979.
script: The statue of Edward VI stands just outside St Thomas’ Hospital over in Lambeth, near the river and not far from the Houses of Parliament. It’s a bit of a nod to Edward’s role in refounding this hospital back in 1551, after it had been shut during the religious upheavals.

name: Robert Clayton
summary: The statue of Robert Clayton stands at the entrance to the North Wing of St Thomas' Hospital, Lambeth, London. The sculptor was Grinling Gibbons, and the statue was executed around 1700–1714. Sir Robert was a banker, politician and Lord Mayor of London. As President of St Thomas', he was responsible for the complete rebuilding of the hospital, and associated church in the late 17th century. The statue was designated a Grade I listed structure in 1979.
script: The Robert Clayton statue stands just outside the North Wing of St Thomas’ Hospital in Lambeth, right across the river from the Houses of Parliament. It’s a proper old carving by the famous Grinling Gibbons, made in the early 1700s. What’s wild is that the statue’s so detailed, you can almost see the tiny veins in Clayton’s hands. It’s like history frozen in stone, right in the city.

name: Stuart Hall Library
summary: The Stuart Hall Library is the special collections library and archive of Iniva (Institute of International Visual Art), in Pimlico, London, independent of, but located on the campus of Chelsea College of Arts.
script: The Stuart Hall Library is a special collections library tucked away in Pimlico, right on the Chelsea College of Arts campus. It’s packed with over 10,000 items focusing on contemporary art from all over the world, especially from African, Caribbean, and Asian artists. What many don’t know is it’s named after Stuart Hall, a brilliant cultural thinker who helped set up the place to celebrate diverse voices in art.

name: Mary Seacole
summary: The statue of Mary Seacole stands in the grounds of St Thomas' Hospital, Lambeth, London. Sculpted by Martin Jennings, the statue was executed in 2016. It honours Mary Seacole, a British-Jamaican who established a "British Hotel" during the Crimean War and who was posthumously voted first in a poll of "100 Great Black Britons".
script: The Mary Seacole statue is just outside St Thomas' Hospital over in Lambeth, right by the Thames and not far from the Eye. She was a remarkable British-Jamaican nurse who set up a "British Hotel" during the Crimean War to look after soldiers, all on her own after being turned away by official nursing groups.

name: Clement Attlee
summary: The statue of Clement Attlee on the Mile End campus of Queen Mary University of London is a bronze sculpture of the British Prime Minister, created by Frank Forster in 1988. The statue was commissioned by the Greater London Council and was intended to stand in Mile End Park. By the time of its completion in 1988, the GLC had been abolished and the statue was offered to any successor authority willing to pay the relocation costs. These were met by Tower Hamlets London Borough Council and the statue was erected outside the Limehouse Public Library to commemorate Attlee's role as the member for the Limehouse parliamentary constituency. The opening ceremony was carried out by Harold Wilson, the last living member of Attlee's 1945-51 administration. By the 21st century, the statue had been badly vandalised and was boarded up. In 2010, Tower Hamlets Council offered the statue to Queen Mary University of London on permanent loan. It was re-erected on a site at the Mile End Road campus, next to the People's Palace where Attlee had attended the vote counting in the 1945 general election and learnt of the victory which brought in his peace-time government.
script: The Clement Attlee statue is over at Queen Mary University’s Mile End campus, just east of the City. It’s a bronze sculpture of Attlee, the post-war Prime Minister who brought in the NHS and a whole lot of social change. Funny thing is, the statue was actually meant for Mile End Park, but by the time it was ready in 1988, the council that commissioned it had been scrapped, so it got moved around a bit before settling here.

name: Here
summary: Here is a 2013 artwork created by artist duo Thomson & Craighead. The work, a standard UK road sign pointing northwards, is situated on a riverside path on the west side of the Greenwich Peninsula in south-east London, where it forms part of The Line, a public art trail that very roughly follows the path of the Prime Meridian as it crosses the River Thames.
script: The Here sign is an interesting bit of modern art you’ll find on the west side of the Greenwich Peninsula, just by the Thames in south-east London. It looks like a normal road sign pointing north, but it actually shows the entire distance all the way around the Earth back to that very spot – almost 25,000 miles!

name: Bank of England War Memorial
summary: The Bank of England War Memorial, in the internal Garden Court at the headquarters of the Bank of England in the City of London, commemorates the bank's staff who were killed while serving in the First World War and Second World War.  It includes a bronze sculpture by Richard Reginald Goulden portraying Saint Christopher carrying the Christ Child.  It became a Grade II listed building in 2017.  The surrounding buildings of the bank are separately listed at Grade I.
script: The Bank of England War Memorial is tucked away in the Garden Court inside the Bank’s main building, right in the heart of the City of London. It’s a quiet spot that honours the bank’s own staff who lost their lives in both World Wars, with a striking bronze statue of Saint Christopher carrying the Christ Child.

name: Winnie the Bear
summary: Winnipeg (1914 – 12 May 1934), or Winnie, was the name given to a female black bear that lived at London Zoo from 1915 until her death in 1934. Purchased from a hunter by cavalry veterinarian Harry Colebourn, Winnie is best-remembered for inspiring the name of A. A. Milne and E. H. Shepard's character, Winnie-the-Pooh.
script: The Winnie the Bear story is a right charming bit of London Zoo history, just off Regent’s Park in central London. Winnie was a real black bear who came all the way from Canada during World War I with a soldier called Harry Colebourn, and she ended up inspiring the famous Winnie-the-Pooh, believe it or not. Most folks don’t realise she was actually a mascot for the Canadian cavalry before becoming a beloved zoo resident.

name: Guy the Gorilla
summary: Guy the Gorilla (1946–1978) was a western lowland gorilla (Gorilla gorilla gorilla) who was London Zoo's most famous resident and often profiled on children's TV shows and natural history productions. The exact day of Guy's birth was unknown, but his official birthday was set by the Zoo as May 30, and he received large numbers of cards each year.
script: The Guy the Gorilla statue is just outside London Zoo in Regent’s Park, right in the heart of the city. Guy was the zoo’s most famous resident, arriving way back in 1947 on Guy Fawkes Night, which is how he got his name—bit of a historical nod there. What many don’t know is that despite all the effort to find him a mate, Guy lived most of his life alone and sadly never had any baby gorillas.

name: Riverside Studios
summary:
Riverside Studios is an arts centre on the north bank of the River Thames in Hammersmith, London, England. The venue plays host to contemporary performance, film, visual art exhibitions and television production.
Having opened in May 1976 (1976-05), the original building closed for redevelopment in September 2014 (2014-09). A new Riverside Studios reopened on its original site in August 2019. In March 2023, the Riverside Trust announced it was placing the theatre into administration because of debt incurred. In January 2025, it was announced that Riverside Studios had been purchased and will be operated by the Anil Agarwal Riverside Studios Trust.
script: The Riverside Studios is a creative hub right on the north bank of the Thames in Hammersmith, where you’ll find all sorts of performances, films, and art exhibitions happening. What many don’t realise is that before it became this arts centre back in the 70s, it was actually a film studio from the 1930s to the 50s, churning out classic British films. Bit of a glow-up from old iron foundry to arts hotspot, eh?

name: Shrewsbury Barrow
summary: Shrewsbury Barrow is a Bronze Age burial mound (also known as a tumulus) in Shooter's Hill in South East London, in the Royal Borough of Greenwich. It is a Scheduled Monument.
script: The Shrewsbury Barrow is an ancient Bronze Age burial mound sitting up on Shooter’s Hill in Southeast London, near Greenwich. It’s actually the last one left from what used to be a whole group of six barrows, but most were flattened when the area got built over in the 1930s. What’s clever is that these mounds would’ve been clear as day from the bottom of the hill, standing out against the skyline—quite the prehistoric beacon, if you will.

name: Former Whitehall Palace Steps
summary:
The Palace of Whitehall – also spelled White Hall – at Westminster was the main residence of the English monarchs from 1530 until 1698, when most of its structures, with the notable exception of Inigo Jones's Banqueting House of 1622, were destroyed by fire. Henry VIII moved the royal residence to Whitehall after the old royal apartments at the nearby Palace of Westminster were themselves destroyed by fire. Although the Whitehall palace has not survived, the area where it was located is still called Whitehall and has remained a centre of the British government.
Whitehall was at one time the largest palace in Europe, with more than 1,500 rooms, before itself being overtaken by the expanding Palace of Versailles, which was to reach 2,400 rooms. At its most expansive, the palace extended over much of the area bordered by Northumberland Avenue in the north; to Downing Street and nearly to Derby Gate in the south; and from roughly the elevations of the current buildings facing Horse Guards Road in the west, to the then banks of the River Thames in the east (the construction of Victoria Embankment has since reclaimed more land from the Thames)—a total of about 23 acres (9.3 ha). It was about 710 yards (650 m) from Westminster Abbey.
script: The Former Whitehall Palace Steps are right in the heart of London, near Westminster, where the old royal palace once stood before it was mostly destroyed by fire in 1698. The palace used to be massive—once the biggest in Europe, with over 1,500 rooms, which is wild to think about considering there’s only government buildings here now. Oddly enough, the only part left standing is the Banqueting House, designed by Inigo Jones, which survived the blaze.

name: Texas Legation
summary:
A Texas Legation was maintained by the Republic of Texas in Washington, D.C.; London; and Paris (1 Place Vendôme) from 1836 through 1845.
In a bid to protect itself from almost certain invasion by forces from neighboring Mexico, the Texas government sought to foster international ties and so opened the Texas Legations in London and Paris.  
When Texas sought to join the United States in 1845, the British Empire supported keeping it independent. The British even offered to guarantee Texas's borders with both the United States and Mexico. Texas was a tactical ally of Britain, which wanted a counterweight to the United States. Nonetheless, an independent Texas was probably inviable for financial reasons, and when the republic became a state in 1845, the legations were shut down.
script: The Texas Legation was the official office for the Republic of Texas way back in the 1830s and 40s, right near St. James's Palace in central London. It’s tucked away in a little alley called Pickering Place, sharing a building with Berry Bros. & Rudd, the posh wine merchants that have been there for over 300 years.

name: Time & Tide Bell
summary:
Time and Tide Bell is an art project made up of bells, designed by UK sculptor Marcus Vergette and Australian bell designer Neil McLachlan, installed at coastal locations in the UK.  The first one was placed at Appledore, Devon, in 2009 and the seventh at Mablethorpe, Lincolnshire in June 2019. As of 2021 at least six further bells are planned, and funding obtained from the National Lottery Heritage Fund in 2018 will allow for up to sixteen bells in all to be installed.
Each bell rings around high tide; the bells provide a reminder that rising sea levels caused by climate change will make the pattern of their ringing change. There is every chance that some of the bells will have to be relocated in the twenty-first century.
script: The Time & Tide Bell is a clever art installation found on a few coastal spots around the UK, not right here in London, but it’s a neat bit of British creativity linked to the sea. Each bell rings only at high tide, reminding us that the sea level’s slowly creeping up thanks to climate change, so the bells’ ringing times will shift over the years.

name: Pullens Estate
summary: The Pullens Buildings, also known as the Pullens Estate, are some of the last Victorian tenement buildings surviving in London, England. In the Walworth, Newington area, they are near Elephant and Castle and Kennington Underground stations. Located in Amelia Street, Crampton Street, Iliffe Street, Penton Place and Peacock Street, they are protected by Conservation Area status granted by Southwark Council.
script: The Pullens Estate is a cluster of old Victorian tenement buildings just south of Elephant and Castle, in the Walworth area of London. It’s quite special because it’s one of the last places where you can see workers’ flats attached to workshops, all built by a guy called James Pullen back in the late 1800s.

name: Southwark
summary:
Southwark (  SUDH-ərk) is a district of Central London situated on the south bank of the River Thames, forming the north-western part of the wider modern London Borough of Southwark. The district, which is the oldest part of South London, developed due to its position at the southern end of the early versions of London Bridge, for centuries the only dry crossing on the river. Around 43 AD, engineers of the Roman Empire found the geographic features of the south bank here suitable for the placement and construction of the first bridge.
London's historic core, the City of London, lay north of the bridge and for centuries the area of Southwark just south of the bridge was partially governed by the City, while other areas of the district were more loosely governed. The section known as Liberty of the Clink became a place of entertainment. By the 12th century Southwark had been incorporated as an ancient borough, and this historic status is reflected in the alternative name of the area, as Borough.  The ancient borough of Southwark's river frontage extended from the modern borough boundary, just to the west of the Oxo Tower, to St Saviour's Dock (originally the mouth of the River Neckinger) in the east. In the 16th century, parts of Southwark near London Bridge became a formal City ward, Bridge Without.
The urban area expanded over the years and Southwark was completely separated administratively from the now small City in 1900, although some remnants of City administration remain in the Guildable Manor. Like other parts of London, it now falls under the Mayor of London and London Assembly in addition to its Burough authority. Local points of interest include Southwark Cathedral, Borough Market, Shakespeare's Globe theatre, The Shard, Tower Bridge, Butler's Wharf and the Tate Modern museum.
script: The Southwark is a lively district just south of the Thames, right by London Bridge, known for its mix of history and modern buzz. It’s actually the oldest part of South London, growing up around the first ever London Bridge built by the Romans way back in 43 AD.

name: Charles I
wiki_tag: en:Equestrian statue of Charles I, Charing Cross
summary:
The equestrian statue of Charles I at Charing Cross, London, England, is a work by the French sculptor Hubert Le Sueur, probably cast in 1633 during Charles’ lifetime. It is the oldest bronze statue in London and is considered the central point of the city.
Its location at Charing Cross is on the former site of the most elaborate of the Eleanor crosses erected by Edward I, which had stood for three and a half centuries until 1647. Charing Cross is used to define the centre of London and a plaque by the statue indicates that road signage distances to London are measured from this point. The statue faces down Whitehall towards Charles I's place of execution in 1649 at Banqueting House.
The first Renaissance-style equestrian statue in England, it was commissioned by Charles's Lord High Treasurer Richard Weston for the garden of his country house in Roehampton, Surrey (now in South London). Following the English Civil War the statue was sold to a metalsmith to be broken down, but he hid it until the Restoration. It was installed in its current, far more prominent location in the centre of London in 1675, and the elaborately carved plinth dates from that time.
script: The Charles I statue stands right at Charing Cross, smack in the middle of London, where all the distances to the city get measured from. It's actually London’s oldest bronze statue, cast while the king was still alive back in the 1630s. What’s a bit wild is that after Charles was executed, the statue was nearly melted down during the Civil War, but some clever bloke hid it away until the monarchy got restored.

name: George IV
wiki_tag: en:Equestrian statue of George IV, Trafalgar Square
summary: The statue of George IV in Trafalgar Square, London, is a bronze equestrian statue by Sir Francis Legatt Chantrey. It depicts the King dressed in ancient Roman attire and riding bareback. The sculpture was originally designed to sit on top of the Marble Arch at the entrance to Buckingham Palace, but was placed in its current location following the King's death.
script: The George IV statue you see here in Trafalgar Square is a bronze figure of the King dressed up like an ancient Roman emperor, riding bareback on his horse. It wasn’t always meant to be here – originally, it was supposed to sit on top of Marble Arch, right outside Buckingham Palace, but after the King died, they stuck it here instead, more or less as a placeholder.

name: Tommy Flowers
summary: Thomas Harold Flowers (22 December 1905 – 28 October 1998) was an English engineer with the British General Post Office. During World War II, Flowers designed and built Colossus, the world's first programmable electronic computer, to help decipher encrypted German messages.
script: The Tommy Flowers was a clever bloke from East London who built the world’s first programmable electronic computer during World War II, right here in Britain. He worked for the Post Office and designed Colossus to crack those tricky German codes, which was top secret for years. What’s mad is, despite his massive contribution, his work stayed under wraps for decades, so most Londoners didn’t even know about him.

name: Honourable Artillery Company Museum
summary: The Honourable Artillery Company Museum opened in 1987 in Armoury House, City Road, London, England. It is associated with the Honourable Artillery Company, the oldest regiment in the British Army, which still maintains an active regiment as a core part of today's Army Reserve.
script: The Honourable Artillery Company Museum is tucked away on City Road, not far from the bustling heart of London, and it’s all about the oldest regiment in the British Army, which still serves today in the Army Reserve. What’s quite surprising is that the museum isn’t just for anyone wandering past – it’s only open to members of the company and their guests, so it’s a bit of a secret club, really.

name: Revolving Torsion
summary:
Revolving Torsion is a 1972–73 kinetic sculpture and fountain by the Russian-born Constructivist artist Naum Gabo. It was commissioned for the Tate Gallery and has been on long-term loan to the Guy's and St Thomas' Charity for display at St Thomas' Hospital in Lambeth, London, since 1975. It was given Grade II* listed status in January 2016.
The sculpture is the culmination of an idea that Gabo developed in the mid-1920s to implement the ideas published in his 1920 Realistic Manifesto. He made a series of models and maquettes over the years, including his work of c. 1929 Model for "Torsion", a small 10 centimetres (3.9 in)-high Perspex model; his larger work Torsion from 1929–37, a 35 centimetres (14 in)-high model also in Perspex; and his 1960–64 Torsion (Project for a Fountain), an 80 centimetres (31 in)-high bronze maquette.
A commission was suggested by Sir Norman Reid, director of the Tate Gallery, when he saw the models on a visit to Gabo's studio in the United States in 1968. Gabo sent his maquette to London and the full-size sculpture was constructed of several stainless steel plates, creating a stack of intersecting curves, deliberately unadorned and without colour. The sculpture was manufactured in 1972–73 by Stainless Metalcraft Limited of London, paid for by Alistair McAlpine, and then donated to the Tate Gallery. Gabo donated his bronze maquette to the Tate Gallery in 1969 and two plastic models in 1977.
The work was installed in 1975 in the centre of a circular pool of water in a square garden at St Thomas' Hospital, with the River Thames to the west and Westminster Bridge Road to the north, and new hospital buildings to the east and south.  It is a working fountain, with water emitted in streams from some of the sculpture's curved edges.  It was originally designed to rotate slowly, once every 10 minutes, but the mechanism has not worked for several years.
script: The Revolving Torsion is a kinetic sculpture and fountain just by St Thomas' Hospital down in Lambeth, near the River Thames. It was made in the early 70s by this Russian artist called Naum Gabo, who was all about shapes and movement—he even planned it back in the 1920s! Originally, the whole thing was meant to slowly spin around every ten minutes, but that clever mechanism hasn’t worked for years now, so it’s more of a still beauty these days.

name: Queen Elizabeth Hall
summary:
The Queen Elizabeth Hall (QEH) is a music venue on the South Bank in London, England, that hosts classical, jazz, and avant-garde music, talks and dance performances. It was opened in 1967, with a concert conducted by Benjamin Britten.
The QEH was built along with the smaller Purcell Room as part of Southbank Centre arts complex. It stands alongside the Royal Festival Hall, which was built for the Festival of Britain of 1951, and the Hayward Gallery which opened in 1968.
script: The Queen Elizabeth Hall is a music venue right on the South Bank, just near the Thames and not far from the Royal Festival Hall. It opened back in ’67 and hosts all sorts—classical, jazz, even some proper experimental stuff. What most folks don’t realise is it’s built on the site of an old lead shot tower from the 1800s, so it’s got a bit of industrial history tucked away beneath all the artsy vibes.

name: William Morris Society
summary:
Kelmscott House is Grade II* listed Georgian brick mansion at 26 Upper Mall in Hammersmith, overlooking the River Thames. Built in about 1785, it was the London home of English textile designer, artist, writer and socialist William Morris from 1878 to 1896.
Originally called The Retreat, Morris renamed it after the Oxfordshire village of Kelmscott, where he had leased Kelmscott Manor as a country retreat since June 1871.
Nearby, Morris began his "adventure in printing" with his private press, the Kelmscott Press, which he started at 16 Upper Mall in 1891.
script: The William Morris Society is based at Kelmscott House, a lovely Georgian mansion right by the Thames in Hammersmith, west London. It was the London home of William Morris, the famous designer and socialist, back in the late 1800s. Now, here’s a bit you might not know—before Morris moved in, the place was owned by Sir Francis Ronalds, who built the first electric telegraph in the garden, way ahead of his time.
